hints: Think about why $\text{AlCl}_3$ dimerises, count the electrons around Al in the monomer and what Al needs to complete its octet.
Consider which atoms can donate a lone pair to form the bridges, and how you would distinguish those dative bonds from normal covalent bonds in your sketch.
walkthrough:
See why the monomer cannot survive alone**
In $\text{AlCl}_3$, Al has only 3 bonding pairs, so 6 electrons in its outer shell. It is electron deficient and wants 8. A lone pair from a Cl on a neighbouring molecule can be donated in to fill that gap, so two molecules join together to share two Cl bridges.

Build the bridged shape**
Draw two Al atoms side by side. Put one Cl above and one Cl below, each bonded to both Al atoms to make a central four membered $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_2$ ring. Then add two terminal Cl atoms to each Al, one up and out, one down and out. Each Al is now surrounded by 4 bonds.

Show the dative bonds clearly**
Each bridging Cl already has a normal covalent bond to one Al, but uses a second lone pair to form a coordinate bond to the other Al. Show this by drawing an arrow from the bridging Cl lone pair pointing towards Al for the two dative bonds. That arrow direction is what earns the second mark.

Final answer: Dimer $\text{Cl}_2\text{Al}(\mu\text{-Cl})_2\text{AlCl}_2$ with two bridging Cl atoms linking the two Al atoms, each Al also bonded to two terminal Cl atoms.
Two Al-Cl bridging bonds shown as coordinate / dative bonds with arrows pointing from Cl to Al.

hints: Count the bonding pairs and lone pairs on Al in gaseous $\text{AlCl}_3$ and recall the shape that minimises repulsion for that number.
walkthrough:
Apply VSEPR to the monomer**
In $\text{AlCl}_3(g)$, Al has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs. Three regions repel equally to give a trigonal planar shape, so the $\text{Cl-Al-Cl}$ angle is $120^{\circ}$.

hints: Write the full atom configurations for Li (3 electrons) and H (1 electron), then adjust for loss or gain of one electron.
walkthrough:
Lose and gain to reach helium**
Li is $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^1$, so losing the outer $2\text{s}$ electron leaves $\text{Li}^{+}$ as $1\text{s}^2$. H is $1\text{s}^1$, so gaining one electron gives $\text{H}^{-}$ as $1\text{s}^2$. Both ions end up with the stable helium configuration.
Final answer: $\text{Li}^{+}$ is $1\text{s}^2$ and $\text{H}^{-}$ is $1\text{s}^2$

hints: Picture what particles remain when metal atoms lose their outer electrons, and where those electrons go.
walkthrough:
Picture the sea of electrons**
Think of LiAl as positive ions packed in a regular lattice. Their outer electrons are no longer attached to any one atom but are free to move throughout the whole structure. The strong electrostatic attraction between the cations and this mobile sea of delocalised electrons is metallic bonding.
Final answer: Lattice of cations / positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.

hints: Focus on the clue that the white solid dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH}$, recall which metal hydroxides are amphoteric.
walkthrough:
Use the excess alkali clue**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ contains Al, so the Al containing product in water must be a hydroxide. Most hydroxides are insoluble white solids, but only amphoteric ones like $\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3$ redissolve in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to form $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^{-}$. That matches exactly, so the precipitate is $\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3$.
Final answer: $\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3$ / aluminium hydroxide

hints: Look at butane-1,2-diol and product P, decide which alcohol is oxidised to which functional group and whether you need mild or vigorous oxidation.
Recall the standard strong oxidising mixture for converting a primary alcohol fully to a carboxylic acid while also oxidising a secondary alcohol.
walkthrough:
Read what changes in reaction 1**
Butane-1,2-diol has a primary $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and a secondary $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$. In P, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOOH}$, the primary end has become $-\text{COOH}$ and the secondary centre has become a ketone $\text{C=O}$. Both need strong oxidation.

Choose the vigorous oxidant and conditions**
That double oxidation needs hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 / \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. You must heat under reflux so volatile aldehyde intermediates are kept in the flask and fully oxidised to the acid and ketone without distilling off.
Final answer: Potassium dichromate(VI) acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, heat under reflux.

hints: Compare structures of P, Q and the target 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, decide which functional groups must be reduced and which must be left alone.
Recall the key difference in reducing power between $\text{LiAlH}_4$ and $\text{NaBH}_4$ toward $\text{C=O}$ in ketones versus $\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Spot what must happen**
P is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOOH}$. To get 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$, you must reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol but leave the carboxylic acid untouched.

Match the reagent to the selectivity**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ is very powerful and reduces almost everything, including $\text{COOH}$ to primary alcohol, so Q is over reduced and is a diol. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is milder, it reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids. So only reaction 3 with $\text{NaBH}_4$ gives the desired R.

Final answer: R is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid as only the ketone $\text{C=O}$ is reduced in reaction 3.
$\text{NaBH}_4$ is a weaker reducing agent and cannot reduce $\text{COOH}$ / carboxylic acid, whereas $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is strong enough to reduce both ketone and $\text{COOH}$.

hints: Identify the true nucleophile supplied by the $\text{NaCN/HCN}$ mixture and why $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks rather than $\text{HCN}$.
Look at the polarity of the $\text{C=O}$ bond in propanal to decide where the nucleophile attacks and where the pi electrons move.
Think about what charge the oxygen carries after the pi bond breaks, and what the carbon skeleton of that intermediate looks like.
Remember to show lone pairs, full and partial charges, and to draw each curly arrow from electron source to electron destination.
walkthrough:
Start with the right attacker**
$\text{HCN}$ is a weak acid, but $\text{CN}^{-}$ from $\text{NaCN}$ is the strong nucleophile. Draw $:\text{C}\equiv\text{N}:^{-}$ with its lone pair on carbon clearly shown. Carbon attacks because it carries the negative charge and lone pair.

Polarise the carbonyl**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so mark $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{CN}^{-}$ lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto oxygen. Arrows must start at the electrons and end at the atom.

Draw the alkoxide intermediate**
After attack, carbon is now bonded to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, H, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{O}^{-}$. Draw $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{O}^{-})\text{CN}$ with a full negative charge and three lone pairs on oxygen. Later protonation by $\text{HCN}$ gives the cyanohydrin S, but this anionic intermediate is the key marking structure.

Final answer: Nucleophile is $:\text{CN}^{-}$ with $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond shown.
Curly arrow from $\text{CN}^{-}$ lone pair to carbonyl C of propanal, with $\text{C}^{\delta+}$-$\text{O}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown and curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O.
Intermediate $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{O}^{-})\text{CN}$ formed.

hints: Balance atoms for hydrolysis of $-\text{CN}$ to $-\text{COOH}$ in acid, remembering $\text{NH}_3$ formed is protonated to $\text{NH}_4^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the nitrile in acid**
Heating the cyanohydrin with aqueous $\text{HCl}$ adds two water molecules across $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to give the carboxylic acid plus ammonia. In acid the ammonia becomes $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$. So add $\text{HCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the left and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ on the right: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN} + \text{HCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

hints: Scan the spectrum above $1500\text{ cm}^{-1}$ and list the sharp peak near $2200\text{ cm}^{-1}$ and the broad features near $3300$ and $3000\text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Recall the characteristic IR ranges for $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, $\text{C=O}$ in acids, and very broad $\text{O-H}$ in $\text{RCO}_2\text{H}$, then decide which molecule fits all the evidence.
walkthrough:
Spot the nitrile fingerprint**
There is a sharp absorption at about $2200\text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is the classic $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ stretch. 2-hydroxybutanoic acid has no nitrogen, so this alone points strongly to the cyanohydrin S.

Confirm by what is missing**
There is no strong peak at 1680-1730 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ where a carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$ would appear, and no very broad absorption at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{O-H}$ in $\text{RCO}_2\text{H}$. The broad band near $3200$-$3400\text{ cm}^{-1}$ is just the alcohol $\text{O-H}$ in S. Any two of these observations prove the compound is S.

Final answer: Compound is S.
Absorption at 2200-2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ shows presence of $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ AND lack of absorption at 1680-1730 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ shows absence of $\text{C=O}$ / lack of absorption at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ shows absence of $\text{O-H}$ in $\text{RCO}_2\text{H}$. (Any two correct references)
